# Differential prevalence {#sec-differential-prevalence}

Differential prevalence analysis (DPA) compares the presence/absence of taxa,
instead of their abundances, between groups. Based on recent studies on the
classification accuracy of healthy vs. non-healthy individuals, a high
proportion of the information in microbiome data seems to be included in the
mere presence/absence of taxa [@Giliberti2022; @Karwowska2025]. DPA is thus a
viable, and even simpler, alternative to differential abundance analysis
(DAA, @sec-differential-abundance). It has also given replicable results in a
benchmark study [@Pelto2025].

Because the detection (observed presence) of a taxon depends on the
sequencing depth, DPA should control for it. In this chapter, we show how to
perform DPA with logistic regression (@sec-DPA), with the Bayesian method
DiPPER (@sec-dpa-dipper) and with Firth logistic regression (@sec-dpa-firth).

## Preparing the data {#sec-dpa-prepare}

We use the same Tengeler2020 dataset [@Tengeler2020] as in DAA
(@sec-prepare-data), and prepare it in the same way: the data is
agglomerated to the genus level and filtered by a prevalence threshold of
10%, and we compare the ADHD and control groups while controlling for
`cohort`.

```{r}
#| label: dpa_prepare_data

library(mia)
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")
tse <- Tengeler2020

# Agglomerate by genus and subset by prevalence
tse <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Genus")
tse <- addPrevalence(tse)
tse <- subsetBy(tse, rows = prevalence > 0.1)

# Transform patient_status to a factor and set "Control" as the reference level
tse$patient_status <- factor(tse$patient_status, levels = c("Control", "ADHD"))

# We also transform cohort as a factor
tse$cohort <- factor(tse$cohort, levels = c("Cohort_1", "Cohort_2", "Cohort_3"))
```

## Logistic regression {#sec-DPA}

We show here how to perform differential prevalence analysis (DPA) with
logistic regression. We show the case where we compare subjects with and
without ADHD while controlling for `cohort`.
Due to the convenient implementation of logistic regression for DPA,
we employ here the `maaslin3()` function from the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("maaslin3")` package [@Nickols2024].

To run the `maaslin3()` function, we need to provide it with

- a `tse` object,
- a model formula, in this case `~ patient_status + cohort + total`, and
- a folder for output files.

Note that we also control for the sequencing depth/library size/total read
count (`total`) in the analysis. This is because the detection
(observed presence) of taxa may depend on the sequencing depth.

```{r}
#| label: run_dpa_cov

library(maaslin3)

# Calculate the sequencing depth (the total number of reads/counts) for each
# sample
tse <- addQC(tse)

# Run maaslin3 with patient_status, cohort and total as the predictor variables
obj_DPA_cov <- maaslin3(
    tse,
    formula = ~ patient_status + cohort + total, # Model formula
    output = "output", # The name of the folder for some output files
    plot_associations = FALSE, # To prevent some unnecessary plots
    plot_summary_plot = FALSE,
    verbosity = "ERROR" # To prevent some unnecessary output
)
```

Next, we extract the `data.frame` of results from the list object returned by
`maaslin3()`. We remove the variable `total` from the output as it is merely a
technical covariate that we are not interested in. Furthermore, as with
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("Maaslin2")`, we calculate the q-values separately for
`patient_status` and `cohort`. Lastly, we keep the most relevant columns.

```{r}
#| label: results_DPA_cov

# Extract the results and calculate the q-values for each variable
res_DPA_cov <- obj_DPA_cov$fit_data_prevalence$results |>
    filter(name != "total") |>
    group_by(metadata) |>
    mutate(qval = p.adjust(pval_individual, method = "fdr")) |>
    ungroup() |>
    select(feature, name, coef, stderr, pval = pval_individual, qval)

# Print the results for taxa with the smallest p-values for patient_status
res_DPA_cov |>
    filter(name == "patient_statusADHD") |>
    arrange(pval) |>
    head() |>
    kable()
```

The results are in the same format as the DAA results in @sec-daa-cov. The
only difference is that `coef` now indicates the log-odds ratio for the
difference in prevalences. The odds ratios (OR) would thus be calculated as
`or = exp(coef)`. Note also that the results are not provided for taxa that
were present in all samples (as it is not sensible to analyze presence/absence
differences for such taxa).

By examining the results we see that the smallest p-value was observed for
genus _Erysipelatoclostridium_. As the sign of the estimate is _negative_, it
means that the genus is more prevalent in the control group. (This can be
seen from the prevalence bars of _Erysipelatoclostridium_ in the strip plots in
@fig-daa-boxplots.)

### With an interaction {#sec-logr-ia}

Contrary to `Maaslin2()`, the `maaslin3()` function also supports the analysis
with interaction terms. Therefore, in the analysis with interaction(s), one can
just add the interaction term(s) into the model formula by
using the standard R syntax, e.g.,
`formula = ~ patient_status + cohort + patient_status:cohort + total` or
alternatively `formula = ~ patient_status * cohort + total`.

## DiPPER {#sec-dpa-dipper}

`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("DiPPER")` [@Pelto2026] is a Bayesian method for DPA
that connects the logistic regression models of the taxa with a common
hierarchical prior. Unlike standard logistic regression, it gives finite
estimates even when a taxon is absent from one group, and its results are
adjusted for multiple testing without a separate q-value correction. It also
supports longitudinal data and works directly with `TreeSE`.

The code below repeats the logistic regression analysis above (@sec-DPA). It
is not run when the book is built, as DiPPER needs the separately installed
[CmdStan](https://github.com/jepelt/DiPPER#installation) backend. Instead,
the results shown below were computed beforehand with DiPPER 0.99.1 (see
`inst/scripts/dipper_precompute.R` in the book repository). The first term of
the formula is the variable of interest.

```{r}
#| label: run_dpa_dipper
#| eval: false

library(DiPPER)

fit_dipper <- dipper(
    tse = tse,
    assay.type = "counts",
    data.type = "counts", # Presence is defined as a count above zero
    formula = ~ patient_status + cohort,
    read.depth = TRUE # Control for the sequencing depth
)

# Results for patient_status: log-odds ratio estimates, 95% credible
# intervals and pseudo q-values
res_dipper <- summary(fit_dipper)

# Forest plot of the taxa whose credible interval excludes zero
plot(fit_dipper)
```

The `summary()` gives log-odds ratio estimates (`log_or`) with 95% credible
intervals (`lwr`, `upr`) and a `pseudo_q` value that resembles a q-value. A
taxon is flagged as `significant` when its credible interval excludes zero.

```{r}
#| label: results_dpa_dipper
#| echo: false

# Precomputed results of summary(fit_dipper)
res_dipper <- read.csv(
    system.file("extdata", "dipper_tengeler2020.csv", package = "OMA")
)

res_dipper |>
    head() |>
    kable()
```

![Differential prevalence between the ADHD and control groups estimated with
DiPPER, controlling for cohort and sequencing depth. The points are the
odds ratio estimates and the lines their 95% credible intervals, shown for the
genera whose interval excludes one. Computed beforehand with
DiPPER 0.99.1.](figures/dipper_tengeler2020.png){#fig-dpa-dipper width="80%"
fig-alt="Forest plot of differential prevalence odds ratios on a log scale with a dashed vertical line at one. Erysipelatoclostridium and the [Ruminococcus] gauvreauii group have odds ratios below one, that is, they are less prevalent in the ADHD group, while Barnesiella and Ruminococcaceae UCG-014 have odds ratios above one."}

As with maaslin3 above, _Erysipelatoclostridium_ has the strongest evidence
for a difference in prevalence, and it is less prevalent in the ADHD group
(@fig-dpa-dipper). See the
[DiPPER vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/DiPPER/inst/doc/DiPPER.html)
for more information.

## Firth logistic regression {#sec-dpa-firth}

While the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("maaslin3")` package provides a convenient
implementation of logistic regression for microbial DPA, we note that it may
provide somewhat conservative results, that is, it rarely provides false
positive results but it may fail to detect some true effects. To obtain higher
statistical power, we recommend using a version of logistic regression
introduced by @Firth1993. As there currently exists no convenient
implementation of Firth logistic regression for DPA, one needs to use a custom
function. Such a custom function with application examples is given in the
[extra materials](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA-extras/docs/devel/pages/extra_daa.html#sec-firth).

## Exercises {#sec-differential-prevalence-exercises}

We use the [`peerj13075`](data_sets.qmd#sec-data-peerj13075) dataset, as in
the exercises of [@sec-differential-abundance].

Solve the exercises in order, as each exercise continues from the previous
one. Try to solve each exercise yourself before opening the solution.

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 1: Prepare the data

**Goal:** Prepare the data for DPA.

1. Load the `peerj13075` dataset from the `mia` package and store it in a
variable called `tse`.

2. Agglomerate the data to genus level with `rank = "genus"`. (Note that the
rank names of this dataset are written in lowercase.) Then add the prevalence
and keep only the genera that are present in more than 50% of the samples.

3. Convert the `Diet` column to a factor and set `Mixed` as the reference
level.

4. Convert the `Geographical_location` column to a factor with the levels
`Pune`, `Ahmednagar` and `Nashik`, in this order. `Pune` is then the
reference level.

**Useful functions:** `data()`, `mia::agglomerateByRank()`,
`mia::addPrevalence()`, `mia::subsetBy()`, `factor()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_dpa_prepare

library(mia)

# 1. Load the data
data("peerj13075", package = "mia")
tse <- peerj13075

# 2. Agglomerate to genus level and keep prevalent genera
tse <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus")
tse <- addPrevalence(tse)
tse <- subsetBy(tse, rows = prevalence > 0.5)

# 3. Set Mixed as the reference level
tse$Diet <- factor(tse$Diet, levels = c("Mixed", "Veg"))

# 4. Set Pune as the reference level
tse$Geographical_location <- factor(
    tse$Geographical_location,
    levels = c("Pune", "Ahmednagar", "Nashik")
)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 2: Logistic regression

**Goal:** Compare the presence and absence of taxa between groups with
`maaslin3()`.

1. Calculate the total number of reads in each sample with `addQC()`. The
results are stored in the `total` column of `colData`.

2. Run `maaslin3()` with `tse` and the formula
`~ Diet + Geographical_location + total`. Set `output = "output"`,
`plot_associations = FALSE`, `plot_summary_plot = FALSE` and
`verbosity = "ERROR"`. Store the result in a variable called `obj_dpa`.

3. Extract the results of the prevalence model (`fit_data_prevalence`).
Remove the rows for `total`, calculate the q-values separately for each
variable, and keep the columns `feature`, `name`, `coef`, `stderr`, `pval`
(renamed from `pval_individual`) and `qval`, as shown in @sec-DPA. Store the table in a variable called
`res_dpa`.

4. Show the six genera with the smallest p-values for `DietVeg`.

5. What does `coef` describe in these results? Why is the total number of
reads included in the model? Why are `coef` and the p-values missing (`NA`)
for some genera?

**Useful functions:** `mia::addQC()`, `maaslin3::maaslin3()`,
`dplyr::filter()`, `dplyr::mutate()`, `dplyr::group_by()`,
`stats::p.adjust()`, `dplyr::ungroup()`, `dplyr::select()`,
`dplyr::arrange()`, `head()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_dpa_maaslin3

library(maaslin3)
library(dplyr)

# 1. Calculate the total number of reads in each sample
tse <- addQC(tse)

# 2. Run maaslin3 with diet, city and total number of reads
obj_dpa <- maaslin3(
    tse,
    formula = ~ Diet + Geographical_location + total,
    output = "output",
    plot_associations = FALSE,
    plot_summary_plot = FALSE,
    verbosity = "ERROR"
)

# 3. Extract the results of the prevalence model
res_dpa <- obj_dpa$fit_data_prevalence$results |>
    filter(name != "total") |>
    group_by(metadata) |>
    mutate(qval = p.adjust(pval_individual, method = "fdr")) |>
    ungroup() |>
    select(feature, name, coef, stderr, pval = pval_individual, qval)

# 4. Genera with the smallest p-values for diet
res_dpa |>
    filter(name == "DietVeg") |>
    arrange(pval) |>
    head()
```

5. In DPA, `coef` is the log-odds ratio of the presence of the genus between
the `Veg` and `Mixed` groups. A positive value means that the genus is
estimated to be more prevalent in the `Veg` group, and a negative value that
it is less prevalent. The odds ratio is `exp(coef)`.

The more reads a sample has, the more likely it is that a taxon is detected.
The total number of reads is therefore included as a technical covariate, so
that differences in sequencing depth do not appear as differences in
prevalence.

For genera that are present in all samples, `coef` and the p-values are
`NA`, because their presence and absence does not vary.
:::
::::
